glossary: desayunos (note): 'swap your toast for spelt and walnut bread, rye bread or sourdough bread' → 'have your toast on spelt and walnut, rye or sourdough bread' (the source means toast made from that bread, not swapping toast for a loaf; also removes the repeated 'bread', which reads more naturally in British English)

suplemento-pan: 'For an extra €0.20, swap your toast for spelt and walnut bread, rye bread or sourdough bread' → 'For an extra €0.20, have your toast on spelt and walnut, rye or sourdough bread' (same fix as the section note, so the two match)
desayuno-mediterraneo: 'half toast (white / seeded)' → 'half-size toast (white / seeded)' ('half toast' isn't natural English; 'media tostada' means a half-size toast, not half a slice)
desayuno-healthy: 'Iberian cured shoulder' → 'Iberian cured pork shoulder' ('shoulder' alone doesn't say what meat it is; paleta ibérica is by definition pork, so no ingredient is added)

merienda: 'Merienda is the Spanish afternoon snack: Cacaolat chocolate milk or juice + …' → 'Afternoon snack: Cacaolat chocolate milk or juice + …' (the full-sentence gloss read like an explanation, not a menu line; the gloss is now shorter and matches the style of the other glosses)
menus (note): 'Toast: avocado / salmon.' → 'Open toast: avocado / salmon.' (tosta is 'open toast' in the section title and in the menu-completo description, so this makes the terms match)

ensalada-cobb: 'Mixed lettuce and shoots' → 'Mixed lettuce and baby leaves' ('brotes' in a Spanish salad means tender baby leaves; 'shoots' is odd here, and 'baby leaves' is the usual British menu wording)

sandwiches (note): "'Toasts & Sandwiches' blackboard" → "'Tostas y Sándwich' blackboard" (this is the name written on the real board in the café, so keeping it lets English readers match the note to the board)
sandwich-salmon: 'Tritordeum sliced bread' → 'Sliced tritordeum bread' (more natural British word order)
sandwich-ventresca: 'Tritordeum sliced bread' → 'Sliced tritordeum bread' (more natural word order, and it now matches sandwich-salmon)

bocadillo-paleta (name): 'Cured shoulder bocadillo' → 'Cured pork shoulder bocadillo' (says what meat it is, and matches the breakfast's 'Iberian cured pork shoulder'; the source has no 'ibérica' here, so 'Iberian' is not added)

bocadillo-paleta (desc): 'Bocadillo: a Spanish baguette sandwich, filled with cured shoulder (paleta)' → 'Bocadillo: a Spanish baguette sandwich' (the filling just repeated the name; now it matches the bocadillo-atun gloss)

ensaimada-plus: "The 'Plus' version of our ensaimada (Mallorcan spiral pastry)" → 'Mallorcan spiral pastry' (the old line was filler that suggested we know what 'Plus' means, and the source doesn't say; icing sugar is left out because we can't confirm the Plus version has it)

empanadillas: 'Baked turnovers' → 'Small savoury turnovers' (the source doesn't say they are baked, and empanadillas can be fried; 'small savoury' is a safe gloss for the diminutive and the savoury fillings)

napolitana-jamon-queso: 'Napolitana: a flat, rectangular pastry made with croissant dough' → 'Napolitana: a flat, rectangular flaky pastry' (Spanish napolitanas are usually made with puff pastry, sometimes croissant dough; 'flaky' is true of both)

cafes (title): 'Coffee, cocoa and herbal teas' → 'Coffee, cocoa and infusions' (té moruno is green tea with mint, not a herbal tea; 'infusions' is faithful to 'infusiones' and is normal on British café menus)
infusiones (name): 'Herbal teas' → 'Tea and infusions' (the list includes té moruno, which is a real tea, so 'herbal teas' mislabels it)
infusiones (desc): 'Moroccan tea' → 'Moroccan mint tea' (the standard English name for té moruno; the mint is part of the drink's definition, not an added ingredient)
colacao: 'Classic Spanish cocoa drink' → 'Spanish cocoa drink' (drops 'Classic', a claim the source doesn't make; now matches the translator's own glossary)
